name: Badrinarayan Temple, Badrinath
deity: Vishnu as Badrinarayan, seated in meditation, with the Goddess Aravindavalli — the Himalayan Divya Desam of Thiruvadari
period: A Divya Desam of Vada Nadu in the Garhwal Himalaya, sung by Periyalvar and Thirumangai Alvar in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham
dynasty: Restored by Adi Shankara by tradition; later Garhwal patronage
summary: High above the Alaknanda at Badrinath, Vishnu is worshipped as Badrinarayan — the Himalayan Divya Desam of Thiruvadari, sung by Periyalvar and Thirumangai Alvar and open only in the summer months.

sections.history: Badrinath is the Thiruvadari, or Badarikashramam, of the Alvars — one of the 108 Divya Desams, the abodes of Vishnu sung in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham, and the Himalayan shrine of Vada Nadu. Periyalvar and Thirumangai Alvar both sang of the Lord of Badari, the latter in two decads of his Periya Thirumozhi. The temple is also one of the Char Dham of India and stands among the Pancha Badri. Tradition credits Adi Shankara, in the eighth or ninth century, with restoring the pilgrimage: he is said to have recovered the image from the Alaknanda and enshrined it beside the hot springs, and the Garhwal kings later cared for the temple. Because of the Himalayan winter, it is open for only about six months of the year.
sections.architecture: The temple rises about fifty feet above the Alaknanda, its stone façade pierced by arched windows and crowned by a small gilded cupola. Pilgrims climb a stair to the brightly painted Singhdwar, the main gate, where a figure of Garuda keeps watch. Within lie the garbhagriha, the darshan mandapa and the sabha mandapa. The image is of black stone, a Shaligram, in a seated, meditative posture. Around it stand shrines of Lakshmi Narasimha, Nara-Narayana, Adi Shankara, Ghantakarna, Vedanta Desika and Ramanuja. Just below flow the Tapt Kund, the hot springs where pilgrims bathe before darshan.
sections.legends: The sthala purana tells that Vishnu performed austerities here, so deep that the Goddess Lakshmi stood over him as a badari, a jujube tree, to shelter him from the cold; from the tree come the name Badri and the name Badrinarayan. Here too, tradition holds, the twin sages Nara and Narayana practised penance, and the two peaks that flank the town bear their names. The Divya Desam lists speak of the Lord as worshipped beneath the jujube tree.
sections.festivals: The year turns on the opening and closing of the temple doors at the start and end of the pilgrim season, each marked with ceremony. The Mata Murti fair in early autumn and the Badri-Kedar festival are customary observances, and in winter the Lord is worshipped lower down the valley at Joshimath. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Badrinath sits in clear, cold air at about 3,100 metres, with the Alaknanda below and the Nara and Narayana peaks on either side. Bathe, if you wish, at the Tapt Kund, then climb to the Singhdwar and join the line for darshan. Come prepared for cold even in summer, and allow for the long mountain road; the journey is itself part of the pilgrimage.

visit.timings: Open only in the pilgrim season, roughly from late April or May to November, with the doors closed through the Himalayan winter; darshan is held daily in the morning and evening. Confirm opening dates and timings locally before travelling.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear removed before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is restricted in and around the sanctum; follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.gettingThere: Badrinath lies on the Alaknanda in Chamoli district, Uttarakhand, about 300 km by road from Rishikesh or Haridwar via Devprayag, Rudraprayag and Joshimath. The nearest railheads are Rishikesh and Haridwar; the nearest airport is Jolly Grant, Dehradun. Mountain roads can close in bad weather, so check conditions before setting out.
